UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION



PJM Interconnection, LLC                              )                Docket No. ER26-3515-000


                    MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF
                     THE NEW JERSEY BOARD OF PUBLIC UTILITIES

          On August 13, 2026, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) proposed revisions to the

Reliability Assurance Agreement Among Load Serving Entities (“RAA”) and the PJM Open

Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) to establish Interim Resource Adequacy Service (“IRAS”).1

On September 3, 2026, the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities (“Board”) submitted its

Supportive Comments and Limited Protest of PJM’s Proposal.2

          Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s

(“Commission” or “FERC”) Rules of Practice and Procedure,3 the Board respectfully moves for

leave to answer and submits this Answer to the protests and comments of Buckeye Power, Inc.

(“Buckeye Power”),4 Southern Maryland Electric Cooperative, Inc. (“SMECO”),5 East Kentucky

     I.   MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER

          While Rule 213(a)(2) generally prohibits answers to protests and comments, good cause

justifies the Commission’s granting this motion and accepting this answer because it provides

useful and relevant information that will assist the Commission in its decision-making process.

    II.   ANSWER

     i.   IRAS Should Not Exceed Amount of New Large Load Demand in Real Time

          Protests and comments submitted by Buckeye Power, SMECO, and EKPC raise issue with

a specific component in PJM’s IRAS Proposal. In its Proposal, PJM proposes to issue load

reductions to electric distribution companies (“EDCs”) in an amount “up to, and capped at, the

pre-Delivery Year IRAS obligations they were assigned” when conducting an IRAS Action.12

 These obligations are pre-determined and correspond to the peak load reported by the New Large

Load in PJM’s proposed Large Load Registry. However, Buckeye Power, SMECO, and EKPC

identify an important concern, which is that this pre-determined amount may not match the actual

New Large Load demand being used in real-time.13 SMECO’s Comments highlight that this is not

merely a hypothetical scenario, as IRAS amounts are set at a pre-Delivery Year MW quantity, yet

an EDC’s assigned New Large Loads may not be yet energized, or may have only just begun a

ramp or testing period that is below its expected draw when PJM issues an IRAS Action.14 If this

is the case and PJM directs an amount of IRAS that corresponds to the peak load reported by the

New Large Load, and this obligation is higher than the real-time demand of large loads in that

zone, it is unclear whether EDCs will be required to reduce other customers in addition to New

Large Load customers in order to meet the required IRAS MW amount. Buckeye Power, SMECO,

and EKPC properly point out that this is clearly not PJM’s intent,15 with Buckeye Power’s

Comments highlighting that “PJM’s goal of ‘prevent[ing] Manual Load Dump’ properly

recognizes that keeping existing customers, particularly residential loads, online is the primary

goal in the event of a grid emergency.”16 Ultimately, however, PJM’s IRAS Proposal does not

provide the clarity needed for EDCs’ IRAS obligations in real-time. To this end, the Board requests

clarification on how PJM will use real-time demand from New Large Loads to inform curtailment

directives, either through a more dynamic database in PJM’s proposed Large Load Registry, or

through the development and maintenance of a different system entirely to assist in this process.

Furthermore, both Buckeye Power and SMECO seek clarification that EDCs will not be required

     ii.   PJM Should Clarify How IRAS Directives Interact with Peak Shaving Adjustments

           The Board appreciates PJM’s consideration of state policies when it added a Peak Shaving

Adjustment (“PSA”) provision in its Reliability Backstop Procurement Proposal (“RBP”) that

would decrement a zone’s RBP obligation commensurate with its PSA arrangements.18 This

provision recognizes the reliability benefits PSA programs provide to the region, and the Board

submitted Comments in appreciation of this component that compliments the newly passed Data

Center Fair Share Act in New Jersey.19          However, while PSA arrangements reduce RBP

obligations, PJM has not explained how they will interact with Bring Your Own New Capacity

(“BYONC”) obligations or IRAS obligations. Several commentators have raised concerns about

this ambiguity.20 The Board likewise seeks clarity regarding how PSA arrangements interact with

IRAS.

           The Board thinks that New Large Loads with PSA agreements must be accounted for

explicitly in PJM’s IRAS operations with real-time information regarding whether New Large

Loads have already reduced their load due to PSA directives. In a scenario in which a New Large

Load has already offset its load due to a PSA directive, it cannot reduce its total registered load

amount in the event the EDC requires it during an IRAS Action. As discussed in reference to

 Buckeye Power’s Comments, it is unclear whether EDCs will face penalties for not curtailing the

entire amount of the registered peak New Large Load amount directed by PJM, or if EDCs must

curtail other customers in order to meet this IRAS obligation.

          The Board recommends that PJM clarify that EDCs will not be required to curtail more

than their New Large Load demand in real time, after accounting for any real-time load reductions

achieved through programs such as PSA. Furthermore, the Board recommends that a more

dynamic data-sharing method is developed for PJM, states, utilities, and New Large Loads to

locate and utilize real-time New Large Load demand, IRAS, and PSA dispatch information for

better information-sharing and accountability. In addition, the Board agrees with Equinix that the

Large Load Registry should account for New Large Loads that are sponsoring PSAs at another site

in the same zone in addition to PSAs associated with the load itself, which is not something PJM’s

Proposal appears to do currently.21

III.      CONCLUSION

          The Board reiterates that it strongly supports PJM’s decision to propose a PJM-led resource

adequacy service for New Large Loads that do not offset their registered peak load with sufficient

capacity arrangements, and thinks its Proposal is largely workable.            However, the Board

underscores concerns other entities have raised and seeks clarity on specific elements that currently

provide confusion and challenges in implementing IRAS.             The Board is hopeful that this

clarification will provide entities in New Jersey with the information they need to effectuate PSA

programs, and that clarification pertaining to the IRAS MW amount will provide EDCs with the

confirmation that they are not expected to curtail other customers during an IRAS Action. The

Board thinks these elements can be addressed without fundamentally altering PJM’s IRAS
